strengths: Addresses a genuine scalability bottleneck in neural causal discovery with substantial practical speedups (4×–13,000×) and enables training on 500-node graphs where prior methods fail
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including multiple baseline paradigms, diverse metrics, thorough ablations, and honest generalization analysis revealing OOD sensitivity
Well-motivated two-stream architecture design with clear justification for each component (reduction on observation dimension, data2graph bridging layer, tied attention weights)
Excellent reproducibility documentation with detailed hyperparameters, training strategy, data generation, hardware specifications, and implementation details in appendix
Scientifically rigorous discussion of limitations and tradeoffs, including candid acknowledgment of lack of DAG enforcement, OOD sensitivity, and limited real-world validation
weaknesses: Critically limited by lack of real-world causal discovery validation—experiments restricted to synthetic and semi-synthetic data with no evaluation on actual biological datasets or established causal benchmarks, severely limiting evidence of practical impact
No enforced acyclicity guarantees; explicitly abandons DAG constraints during prediction, departing from fundamental causal discovery requirements despite paper's framing as 'causal discovery'
Significant performance degradation on out-of-distribution noise distributions and mechanism functions (Figure 6) substantially undermines robustness claims, though sensibly acknowledged

Moderate conceptual novelty—primarily combines existing techniques (pooling, tied attention from prior work, two-stream architectures) without introducing fundamentally new methods or theoretical insights
Unfair baseline comparisons: AVICI evaluated using pre-trained checkpoints while CauScale trains on target data; GRN experiments show AVICI fails entirely preventing actual comparison
Computational cost of computing graph prior ρ at large scale (n=1000) not addressed; potential numerical stability issues for large matrices unexplored despite ablation showing prior importance

Two-stage training strategy (10–100 then 150–500 nodes) suggests architecture doesn't naturally scale, adding implementation complexity for practitioners; scalability claims tested only at single 1000-node point

Strong sample size dependence (Figure 7) with optimal performance at ~2000 samples for synthetic data and ~20000 for GRN indicates method still requires sufficient data; unclear if this limitation is acceptable for target applications
Code availability unclear with incomplete project page, critical for reproducibility and adoption of systems-oriented contribution
Efficiency analysis (Section 4.6) lacks clarity on computational assumptions; no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals reported

strengths: Addresses an important problem of scaling neural causal discovery to large graphs with clear practical motivation
Comprehensive experiments spanning synthetic data with varying sizes, mechanisms, and semi-synthetic gene expression datasets
Significant inference speedups (4×-13,000×) through well-motivated architectural innovations (reduction unit, tied attention, two-stream design)
Detailed ablation studies validating importance of major components (reduction unit, graph stream, attention mechanism)
Strong in-distribution performance on synthetic linear data (99.6% mAP on n=100)
weaknesses: Critical fairness issue: AVICI compared using pre-trained checkpoints from official repository while CauScale is trained on authors' data; this makes the comparison fundamentally unfair and undermines main efficiency claims

Substantial performance degradation on out-of-distribution data contradicts generalization claims: polynomial mechanisms drop from 50.3% (n=100) to 18.9% (n=1000) mAP, barely exceeding baseline performance
Limited real-world applicability: performance on semi-synthetic SERGIO-GRN data (71.4% mAP at n=100) is much lower than on synthetic data; no validation on truly unknown real causal graphs
Reduction unit lacks rigorous justification: no theoretical analysis of information loss from sample-dimension pooling or proof that causal signals are preserved despite aggressive compression

Two-stage training with different batch sizes (8 for n≤100, 1 for n>150) is poorly justified and could harm generalization; training-test scale mismatch (trained on 500 nodes, tested on 1000) not adequately analyzed
Reproducibility concerns: project page URL incomplete, no code availability mentioned, hyperparameter choices appear arbitrary (embedding dimension 128, 16 heads) without justification

Unfair baseline selection: AVICI uses pre-trained weights while SEA is trained on same data; excluding FCI/DiffAN from large-scale experiments 'due to time costs' while including them in 100-node setting is inconsistent

Presentation issues: Figure 1 cluttered and hard to parse, efficiency analysis notation difficult to follow, claims imprecisely stated (e.g., 'one of the first' pre-training studies when AVICI also pre-trains)
No statistical significance testing: results averaged over only 5 graph instances with no error bars or confidence intervals, making reliability assessment impossible
Key design choices lack principled justification: Why inverse covariance for graph prior? Why specific low-rank factorization in data2graph layer? Why not enforce acyclicity if learning DAGs?

strengths: Addresses an important practical problem: scaling causal discovery to large graphs. Successfully trains on 500-node graphs where AVICI fails and enables inference on 1000-node graphs.
Strong empirical results with massive efficiency gains (4×–13,000× speedups) while maintaining high accuracy (99.6% mAP on in-distribution synthetic data, 96.6% on unseen scales, 84.4% on OOD data).

Well-motivated two-stream architecture with clear design rationale: data stream extracts relational evidence from high-dimensional observations while graph stream preserves structural signals. Data-graph block elegantly bridges both streams.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning multiple graph structures (ER, Scale-Free, SBM), causal mechanisms (linear, NN, sigmoid, polynomial), and thorough ablation studies (Figures 3-5) demonstrating that each component contributes meaningfully.
Strong generalization to unseen graph sizes: model trained on graphs up to 500 nodes generalizes to 1000-node test graphs, showing the architecture captures scalable principles.
Excellent reproducibility: detailed appendices cover data generation, baseline implementations, hyperparameter choices, and hardware specifications enabling verification and reproduction.

Sound theoretical efficiency analysis (Section 4.6) providing geometric series justification for time and space complexity improvements, making performance claims more rigorous than typical empirical papers.
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: reduction via pooling is standard, tied attention weights are from prior work (Rao et al., 2021), and two-stream designs are well-established. Main contribution is combining existing techniques—somewhat incremental for a top venue.

Concerning out-of-distribution performance: sharp drop on polynomial mechanisms (50.3% vs. 99.6% on linear), and Figure 6 shows substantially greater sensitivity to OOD noise and mechanisms. This is critical because the core assumption—that synthetic-trained models transfer to real causal mechanisms—remains weakly validated.

Insufficient real-world validation: all experiments use only synthetic or semi-synthetic (SERGIO-GRN) data. SERGIO-GRN accuracy (71.4% mAP for n=100) shows significant drop compared to synthetic (99.6%). No validation on actual biological, medical, or economic datasets despite motivation citing these fields, undermining practical impact claims.

Graph prior contribution inadequately isolated: the inverse covariance prior ρ is structurally informative (similar to GES). Figure 4 shows performance degradation when removed, but the magnitude is unclear and ablation doesn't separate prior contribution from neural architecture contribution. Raises questions about what drives performance.

Training scalability incompletely addressed: requires 39.75 total hours across 8 GPUs with two-stage training and batch size reduction (8→1 for larger graphs), indicating engineering workarounds rather than fundamental scalability. While inference is fast, training is expensive and inelegant.

Cycle control inadequately handled: paper explicitly avoids acyclicity enforcement during prediction. Justification (computational cost, real-world cycles) is weak for causal graph discovery where DAG structure is fundamental. Vanilla head produces up to 0.25% cycles (Figure 5); impact not thoroughly evaluated.

Baseline comparisons have confounds: AVICI uses pre-trained checkpoints rather than fresh training on same data; NOTEARS/SDCD comparisons conflate algorithm type with efficiency (these aren't designed as amortized methods). SEA comparison could be deeper.

Missing error quantification: no error bars or confidence intervals despite averaging over only 5 graph instances. Some differences between methods appear within noise margin. Sharp OOD performance drops lack root-cause analysis.

Incomplete ablations and design justifications: no ablation of data2graph layer design choices (why outer product U*V^T specifically?), limited sensitivity analysis for reduction factor r beyond Section 5.4, no analysis of which graph properties correlate with failure modes.

Limited generalization scope: all test graphs relatively sparse (|E| ∈ {2n, 4n}); no dense graph evaluation or edge-density sensitivity analysis. Unclear if scalability holds across wider parameter ranges.

strengths: Addresses genuine scalability bottleneck in causal discovery with impressive practical results (4×–13,000× speedups, training on 500-node graphs where AVICI fails)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 8 metrics, diverse baselines spanning multiple paradigms, synthetic and semi-synthetic datasets, with thorough ablation studies validating each component
Sound technical approach with clear motivation: reduction along observation dimension (m >> n) and two-stream architecture effectively balance efficiency and information preservation
Strong empirical performance: 99.6% mAP on in-distribution linear data, 84.4% on OOD polynomial data, 96.6% generalization to unseen graph sizes (n=1000 from n≤500 training)
Rigorous efficiency analysis with geometric series derivations showing 36.60% and 48.13% of baseline compute; formal memory complexity proof provided
Well-written with honest limitations discussion; acknowledges reliance on synthetic data and identifies areas for future work
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (reduction pooling, tied attention from Rao et al. 2021, two-stream architecture) without fundamental methodological innovation
No evaluation on real observational data; entirely synthetic/semi-synthetic validation limits assessment of practical applicability. Acknowledged by authors but remains significant gap.

Strong sensitivity to graph prior quality at scale (Table 4): mAP drops to 32.6% for n=1000 with only 10 samples for prior computation; this dependency increases with graph size but receives limited discussion

OOD robustness concerns: cycles emerge in 20-100% of predictions at n=1000 for non-linear mechanisms (Table 2); post-hoc cycle-breaking removes up to 103 edges per graph on average, potentially problematic for downstream applications
Causal sufficiency assumption not thoroughly explored; latent confounder testing (Section 5.6) uses simulation-based node removal rather than genuine confounder scenarios
Code availability unclear: project page link is broken with no explicit release mentioned; reproducibility would be stronger with code
Limited analysis of how method behaves when training distribution diverges from test conditions, particularly important for transfer to real-world applications

strengths: Clear efficiency improvements (4×–13,000× speedups) with rigorous time/space complexity analysis
Ability to scale to 500-node graphs during training (where AVICI OOMs) and infer on 1000-node graphs
Strong in-distribution performance (99.6% mAP on n=100 synthetic data)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with thorough ablations validating each architectural component
Well-written paper with clear presentation, good figures, and detailed implementation information in appendices
Honest discussion of limitations including cycle production, latent confounder sensitivity, and prior dependency
Appropriate impact statement acknowledging ethical considerations
weaknesses: Critical limitation: No evaluation on real-world observational data—only synthetic and semi-synthetic benchmarks. Claims of practical impact are unsupported without real-world causal discovery experiments on genuine observational data

Poor out-of-distribution generalization: 50% mAP drop on polynomial mechanisms (50.3% vs 99.6% for linear at n=100). This brittleness to different causal functions suggests overfitting to training mechanisms and questions the method's generality

Graph prior quality is a critical bottleneck: mAP varies from 32.6% to 64.9% at n=1000 depending on samples used for prior computation. This unpredictable dependency on input data quality limits practical applicability
Cycle production at n=1000 requires post-hoc cycle-breaking heuristic (removing avg 0.4-103 edges). Lack of principled DAG constraint enforcement during training is a fundamental design limitation

Incremental novelty: AVICI (Lorch et al. 2022) already achieved pre-training for amortized causal discovery. CauScale's contribution is primarily engineering (combining reduction units + tied attention + two-stream design) without fundamental algorithmic or theoretical innovation
Severe performance degradation under latent confounding: At h=64 hidden variables, mAP drops substantially, though the authors acknowledge this limitation
Code availability unclear: Project page link is missing, and no explicit commitment to code release limits reproducibility despite detailed documentation
Questionable comparison fairness: AVICI evaluated on pre-trained checkpoints while CauScale trains on target distribution, confounding efficiency comparisons

strengths: Significant practical impact: 4×–13,000× inference speedups and ability to train on 500-node graphs where AVICI fails due to memory constraints
Well-motivated and sound technical design: Each architectural component (reduction unit, tied attention, two-stream design) is justified with clear reasoning and theoretical efficiency analysis

Comprehensive experimental validation: Multiple datasets (synthetic with varying topologies, SERGIO-GRN), diverse causal mechanisms, thorough ablations, and systematic generalization analysis (OOD graphs, noise, mechanisms)
Excellent reproducibility: Detailed implementation specifications, data generation procedures, baseline configurations, and honest hardware requirements enabling full reproduction
Strong in-distribution performance: 99.6% mAP on synthetic data with good generalization to larger graphs (96.6% mAP at n=1000, outside training distribution)
Honest treatment of limitations: Acknowledges causal sufficiency assumptions, latent confounder robustness, graph prior sensitivity, and provides balanced impact statement
weaknesses: Limited real-world validation: Lacks evaluation on actual observational data; SERGIO-GRN is semi-synthetic with significantly lower performance (54%, 39.2% mAP) compared to synthetic (99.6%), raising questions about practical applicability
Training data dependency: Requires pre-training on simulated SCM data; generalization to settings deviating from these assumptions is unclear, as evidenced by large synthetic-to-GRN performance gaps

Out-of-distribution brittleness: Polynomial mechanism at n=1000 achieves only 18.9% mAP (vs 50.3% at n=100); Figure 6 shows greater sensitivity to OOD noise/mechanisms than structures, suggesting fragile learned patterns

Graph prior sensitivity: Section 5.7 reveals increasing sensitivity to prior quality with graph size (32.6% at n=1000 with 10-sample prior vs 64.9% with 500-sample); concerning for limited-sample practical applications
Post-hoc cycle-breaking: The cycle-breaking procedure (removing ~103 edges on average for polynomial) feels unprincipled; better to enforce DAG constraints during training despite computational cost

Limited technical novelty: Reduction unit is straightforward average pooling, tied attention from prior work (Rao et al. 2021), and outer product factorization lacks clear justification; novelty primarily in combination

Missing key comparisons: Training cost comparison with AVICI/SEA not provided (only CauScale: 39.75 hours); hyperparameter sensitivity to k and r not analyzed; prediction head design rationale incomplete
Unexplained performance gaps: Significant drop from synthetic (99.6%) to GRN (54%) at n=100 is not adequately analyzed; unclear if due to mechanism complexity, sample size, or model limitations
